episode_title: Why Interior Designers Choose This Photographer’s Work (George Diebold)
question: Why do interior designers hesitate to specify photography in their designs compared to paintings?
transcript_excerpt: Designers are hung up on the premise that a painting is one-of-a-kind while a photograph can be reproduced multiple times. However, George notes that designers rarely ask him how many copies he makes. The core issue is that many photographers copy successful photographers, resulting in designers seeing repetitive work like another picture of the Grand Canyon or the same Japanese maple tree in the same location, whereas George differentiates himself through both location and studio work with a wider-ranging portfolio.

episode_title: Why Interior Designers Choose This Photographer’s Work (George Diebold)
question: What makes dye sublimation printing on metal superior to plexiglass for fine art photography?
transcript_excerpt: Dye sublimation infuses dyes into metal through extreme heat, making them become part of the metal itself, resulting in extremely archival and durable prints for many years. Unlike laminated plexiglass which is fragile and can fracture at corners, metal prints are highly durable—you can clean them with Windex and a paper towel rather than requiring rubber cement thinner and 100% cotton rags. Metal also offers five to six different levels of reflection from super high gloss to very matte luster.

episode_title: Why Interior Designers Choose This Photographer’s Work (George Diebold)
question: How does George Diebold capture the silky water effect in his Hawaiian wave photographs?
transcript_excerpt: George uses very long camera exposures shot almost in pitch darkness, which allows the water to turn into that silky look. For the photograph behind Gail, he drove about an hour on terrifying narrow, unlit roads with heavy rain and trucks coming at him, set up his equipment, used long exposure photography at dusk, and then had a scary drive back to his condo in the pitch dark.

episode_title: Why Interior Designers Choose This Photographer’s Work (George Diebold)
question: What is George Diebold's philosophy on artwork as investment versus personal enjoyment?
transcript_excerpt: George is brutally honest that investing in artwork is probably not sound criteria when purchasing, as the chances of reselling for more than you paid are unlikely. Instead, he recommends that clients and designers honestly pick things they truly fall in love with and really want, rather than thinking of them as investments. He limits his editions to 8 to 12 pieces and criticizes photographers who reproduce images in hundreds of copies while calling them limited edition, which is almost like a poster.

episode_title: Why Interior Designers Choose This Photographer’s Work (George Diebold)
question: How does AI threaten the fundamental nature of true photography according to George Diebold?
transcript_excerpt: AI has the potential to destroy the very nature of photography because people interested in true photography now must consider whether the situation even existed or ever happened. This is fundamentally contradictory to what photography is—which was invented to record an exact moment in time and preserve an event, person, or place so you could see it exactly as it was. If you alter an image to make something look different from what actually existed, the point of recording that event is lost.
